title: Winter and Room
premise: Folklorist Beatrix Okonkwo returns to the snowbound village of Hollowmere to record its winter songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any of them twice. When her childhood imaginary friend, Winter, appears on her porch unchanged after twenty years, she realizes he is not a memory but a keeper of the village's oldest bargain: something beneath the well was invited in generations ago, and it must be fed a name each winter. As the doors begin to count themselves and the songs rewrite themselves in her recordings, Beatrix must choose between exposing the truth that will free the village and protecting the people who kept her family's name off the list. She survives until sunrise by singing the forbidden song back to the well, un-inviting what was invited — but Winter, bound to the bargain, must go down in her place, and she leaves Hollowmere carrying his last true name.
about_author: Juniper Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist of oral traditions who spent three winters collecting folk songs across northern England and Ireland. They write horror rooted in the belief that every song is a contract, and someone always has to pay.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Beatrix arrives in Hollowmere during the first snow, recording equipment in hand. An old woman sings a harvest song for her, then goes pale and begs her to delete it. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: curiosity shadowed by the first real wrongness.

chapters.title: Doors Counted, Lights On
chapters.summary: Beatrix settles into her late grandmother's cottage and follows old habits: counting doors, checking locks, keeping lamps lit. The count comes out wrong — thirteen doors in an eight-room house. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: unease turning to dread.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: At dusk, Beatrix finds a figure waiting on the porch: Winter, her childhood imaginary friend, exactly as he was at seven years old, untouched by time. He says he's been waiting for her to come home. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into fear.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Friends Remember
chapters.summary: Winter refuses to come inside but knows things he shouldn't — the village's secrets, her grandmother's warnings, the exact wording of an invitation. He warns her: don't sing the songs twice. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: longing for childhood comfort against mounting suspicion.

chapters.title: The Village That Won't Sing
chapters.summary: Beatrix interviews villagers; every one of them stops mid-song when they reach the same verse, as if hitting a wall. The pub landlord tells her the songs were 'paid for' long ago. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: frustration and isolation.

chapters.title: Winter's Side of the Door
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Winter on the porch through the night, revealing he is bound to the cottage threshold and to a bargain older than the village church. He watches something circle the house and counts the lights going out one by one. Emotional beat: protective devotion laced with guilt.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Beatrix finds the old village well, dry for decades, now faintly steaming and rising. In the water she hears harmonies of every song she's recorded, sung slightly wrong. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: revulsion and fascination.

chapters.title: Names on the List
chapters.summary: In her grandmother's locked trunk, Beatrix finds a ledger of names, one crossed out each winter, including her mother's — uncrossed. Winter admits the list is the bargain's payment schedule. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: betrayal by inheritance.

chapters.title: Loyalty of a Made-Up Boy
chapters.summary: Winter confesses he was created by the first bargain as the village's warden — a made-up boy tasked with keeping children from learning their own names are owed. He has loved his charges for two centuries. POV: Winter. Emotional beat: tragic tenderness.

chapters.title: The Verse No One Finishes
chapters.summary: Beatrix reconstructs the missing final verse from fragments across nine recordings. Spoken aloud, it names what was invited in before the well refills: a guest called the Under-Singer, welcomed by the founders in a famine year. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Midnight Choir
chapters.summary: The whole village sleepwalks to the well and sings in unison, faces slack. Beatrix records them; on playback, there is a fourteenth voice. Winter pulls her back before she joins. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: horror of communal complicity.

chapters.title: Duty's Cold Arithmetic
chapters.summary: The village elders confront Beatrix: the bargain keeps everyone alive through winter, and outsiders' questions have 'thinned the walls.' They offer her a place on the council if she burns her recordings. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: temptation of safety versus truth.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Winter shows Beatrix the founding night in a shared vision: starving founders singing a welcome to the Under-Singer, trading one name per winter for survival. The song was never folklore — it was the receipt. POV: shared vision. Emotional beat: grief for the founders' desperation.

chapters.title: The Crossed-Out Name
chapters.summary: Beatrix discovers the most recent crossed-out name belongs to the landlord's daughter, vanished last week and already forgotten by everyone but him. His grief cracks the village's silence. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: righteous anger igniting.

chapters.title: Uninvited Guests
chapters.summary: Because Beatrix recorded the songs, the Under-Singer can now find her. Doors multiply overnight; the thirteenth door opens onto the well itself. Winter holds the threshold all night, weakening. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: siege terror and guilt.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Winter offers to take Beatrix's name onto the list himself — wardens can substitute once. She refuses; he argues duty; she argues love. Neither wins, and dawn finds them still arguing at the threshold. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: fierce, doomed tenderness.

chapters.title: The Longest Night
chapters.summary: Winter solstice: the well refills fully and the village gathers to sing the payment. Beatrix plays her recordings back at the crowd, forcing them to hear the fourteenth voice and remember the landlord's daughter. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: defiance at the brink.

chapters.title: Singing It Backwards
chapters.summary: Climax: Beatrix sings the forbidden song in reverse at the well's edge, un-inviting the Under-Singer while the village, led by the grieving landlord, joins her. The water fights back with every voice it has ever taken. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: desperate, transcendent courage.

chapters.title: A Name Is Owed
chapters.summary: The un-inviting works, but the bargain demands a closing payment. Before Beatrix can speak her own name, Winter speaks his true name — the one he was given at the founding — and steps down into the receding well. POV: Winter. Emotional beat: sacrifice as an act of love.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn comes clean. The well is dry, the doors number eight again, and the villagers weep as memories return. Beatrix stands on the empty porch where Winter waited, holding the ledger with no names left. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: hollow relief and mourning.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: Beatrix archives everything, then listens one final time to her earliest recording: beneath the old woman's harvest song, a child's voice hums a tune she never collected — Winter's tune. She doesn't delete it. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: bittersweet keeping of faith.

chapters.title: Room for Winter
chapters.summary: Leaving Hollowmere, Beatrix passes the well one last time and hears, faintly, a boy humming in harmony with her footsteps. She sets a place for him at every table thereafter, and in the book's final line, counts thirteen doors and smiles. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: love outlasting the bargain.
